sub.en: Look at the pairs. Which action was already in progress, and which one interrupted it?

items.q: I ___ lunch when a man came over.
items.why: The longer action, already in progress, takes the Past Continuous. The short action that interrupts it takes the Past Simple.

items.q: I was having lunch when a man ___ over.
While I ___ to work, I saw the whole thing.
items.why: while goes with the long action; when usually goes with the short one.

items.q: ___ the lift stopped, everybody looked at the floor.
He ___ carefully — he was looking at the table.
What ___ you doing when the lights went out?
I ___ my phone, so I couldn’t call anybody.
items.why: A state — finding, knowing, wanting — takes the simple, not the continuous.

tts: Many of us use lifts several times a day without really thinking about it. But if you watch what people do in lifts, you’ll see some very interesting behaviour. Here to tell us more is psychologist Dr Len Mills.
Yes, that’s right. Lifts are very interesting social spaces. When we’re alone in a lift, we act normally. But when another person comes in, suddenly we behave strangely.
Next time you’re in a lift, watch where people stand. If there are two people, you stand in opposite corners. If a third person enters, you move again, without thinking about it.

tts: Now watch what people do. Some people say hello politely or smile. Others don’t. But everybody turns around as soon as they enter the lift.
Some people look at the door, the floor or at the lift buttons. Others look at their phones, their hands or their ring. But they never make eye contact with the other people.
When two people come in at the same time, they stop their conversation or start speaking quietly.
The reason why we do this is that when we are in small spaces, we feel anxious.

acts.title: Forty-one minutes
text: Aigul was going to a meeting on the ninth floor when the lift stopped between four and five.

At first she wasn’t frightened. She pressed the button on the intercom and a calm voice said somebody was coming. She was reading her notes for the meeting when the lights went out. That was the moment she stopped being calm.

There were two other people inside. Nobody was talking. One man was looking at his phone, although there was no signal; the other was standing exactly in the corner, exactly as far from everybody as the lift allowed. While they were waiting, Aigul noticed that not one of the three of them had made eye contact since the doors closed.
After twenty minutes the man with the phone said, very politely, “I think we should introduce ourselves.” Everybody laughed. They talked for the rest of the time.
The engineers opened the doors forty-one minutes after the lift stopped. Aigul was late for the meeting and, she says, not at all sorry about it.

items.s: The lift stopped between the fourth and fifth floors.

They were inside for forty-one minutes.

write.q: Describe a moment when something interrupted you: 6 sentences. Use two sentences with “I was …-ing when…”, one with “While…”, two adverbs of manner, and say how you felt.
write.model: I was cooking dinner when the electricity went off in the whole street. At first I wasn’t worried. While I was looking for candles, my neighbour knocked very loudly on the door — she wanted to know if it was only her flat. We stood in the corridor and talked calmly about nothing for twenty minutes. I felt embarrassed later, because I still had my apron on. The lights came back at nine.

speak.q: Tell your interruption story out loud in four sentences. Use “I was …-ing when…” at least twice and finish by saying how you felt.
speak.model: I was cooking when the electricity went off. While I was looking for candles, my neighbour knocked on the door. We were standing in the corridor when the lights came back. I felt slightly ridiculous.
